title: Azielon PMP Diagram Library v1
purpose: Structured diagram inventory for PMP study, future app integration, and later image generation.

items.title: Maslow’s Hierarchy of Needs
items.whatItIs: A five-level model of human needs moving from physiological and safety needs up to belonging, esteem, and self-actualization.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for people-domain questions about motivation, morale, recognition, safety, and what type of support a team member most needs.
items.howToReadIt: Read it from bottom to top. Lower layers represent foundational needs; upper layers represent growth and fulfillment.
items.commonTrap: Students often jump to recognition or growth when the scenario actually shows a lower-level need such as safety or job security.
items.memoryHook: Maslow = lower needs first, higher growth later.

items.title: Tuckman Team Development Ladder
items.whatItIs: A staged model showing Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing, and Adjourning.
items.whyItMatters: Important for recognizing normal team behavior and selecting the right leadership response for team maturity.
items.howToReadIt: The team progresses through stages, though it can regress after major changes. Storming is conflict; Norming is alignment; Performing is high productivity.
items.commonTrap: Storming is often mistaken for failure when it may simply be a normal development stage.
items.memoryHook: Tuckman = understand the stage before choosing the response.

items.title: Stakeholder Power/Interest Grid
items.whatItIs: A four-quadrant stakeholder map classifying stakeholders by power and interest: Manage Closely, Keep Satisfied, Keep Informed, and Monitor.
items.whyItMatters: One of the most useful visual tools for stakeholder engagement strategy.
items.howToReadIt: Locate the stakeholder by their power and interest, then apply the matching engagement approach.
items.commonTrap: Power is not the same as interest. Learners often classify a stakeholder correctly but choose the wrong engagement strategy.
items.memoryHook: Power + interest = engagement strategy.

items.title: Stakeholder Engagement Assessment Matrix
items.whatItIs: A matrix comparing current stakeholder engagement against desired engagement states such as unaware, resistant, neutral, supportive, and leading.
items.whyItMatters: Useful when a PMP question asks how to close engagement gaps rather than just classify stakeholders.
items.howToReadIt: Compare current to desired states and identify which stakeholders need a tailored engagement response.
items.commonTrap: This is different from the power/interest grid: this one tracks engagement level, not classification by influence.
items.memoryHook: Power/interest tells who they are; engagement matrix tells how they’re behaving now.

items.title: Conflict Resolution Modes Map
items.whatItIs: A visual comparison of collaborate/problem solve, compromise, smooth/accommodate, force/direct, and withdraw/avoid.
items.whyItMatters: Useful because many tricky PMP questions hinge on which conflict approach is most appropriate.
items.howToReadIt: Read across each mode for intent and typical use. Collaborate aims for win-win; compromise splits the difference; force is urgent/one-sided.
items.commonTrap: Compromise is often mistaken for collaboration.
items.memoryHook: Collaborate solves; compromise settles.

items.title: Power Types Map
items.whatItIs: A comparison chart of expert, referent, legitimate, reward, and coercive power.
items.whyItMatters: Useful in questions about influence, leadership, and stakeholder/team dynamics.
items.howToReadIt: Read each power type by source of influence and likely PMP-favored usage.
items.commonTrap: Expert and referent power are often confused because both are personal forms of influence.
items.memoryHook: Expert = what you know; referent = how people regard you.

items.title: RACI / Responsibility Assignment Matrix
items.whatItIs: A chart assigning who is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted, and Informed for work items.
items.whyItMatters: Very helpful when a question tests role clarity, escalation, and handoffs.
items.howToReadIt: Read each task row across roles, paying special attention to the difference between Responsible and Accountable.
items.commonTrap: Learners often think Responsible and Accountable are interchangeable.
items.memoryHook: Responsible does; Accountable owns.

items.title: Communication Channels Growth Diagram
items.whatItIs: A simple formula-based visual showing that channels grow rapidly as team size increases: n(n−1)/2.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for questions about communication complexity and the need for structured communication planning.
items.howToReadIt: Read the relationship between team size and number of channels, not just the formula.
items.commonTrap: The formula is easy to memorize but students miss the managerial implication: more people means much higher coordination complexity.
items.memoryHook: More people = many more channels.

items.title: Scrum Roles & Ceremonies Flow
items.whatItIs: A process diagram showing Product Owner, Scrum Master, Developers, and the flow through Sprint Planning, Daily Scrum, Sprint Review, and Retrospective.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for distinguishing who owns product value, who facilitates, and what each ceremony is for.
items.howToReadIt: Read the roles first, then the sprint-event flow. Review focuses on product/stakeholders; retrospective focuses on team process.
items.commonTrap: Review and Retrospective are commonly confused.
items.memoryHook: Review = product; Retro = process.

items.title: Context Diagram
items.whatItIs: A high-level visual showing the system or product in the center and its external users, systems, and interfaces around it.
items.whyItMatters: Excellent for PMP questions about scope boundaries, external interfaces, and stakeholder interactions.
items.howToReadIt: Read from the center outward. The key is identifying what is inside the boundary versus what interacts from outside.
items.commonTrap: Students confuse it with a process map. A context diagram shows relationships/boundaries, not detailed process sequence.
items.memoryHook: Context = what surrounds and touches the system.

items.title: Fishbone / Ishikawa Diagram
items.whatItIs: A cause-and-effect diagram used to explore possible root causes of a problem.
items.whyItMatters: Commonly used in quality and root-cause analysis questions.
items.howToReadIt: Start at the effect/problem and read the major cause branches to identify likely root causes.
items.commonTrap: Learners sometimes treat it like a prioritization tool. It helps explore causes; it does not rank them by itself.
items.memoryHook: Fishbone = why did this happen?

items.title: Pareto Chart
items.whatItIs: A bar chart ordered from most frequent/significant cause to least, often paired with the 80/20 principle.
items.whyItMatters: Useful when deciding which defect source or issue category to address first.
items.howToReadIt: Read bars from highest to lowest and identify the few causes producing most of the impact.
items.commonTrap: Students may confuse it with a histogram. Pareto orders categories by significance.
items.memoryHook: Pareto = biggest contributors first.

items.title: Control Chart
items.whatItIs: A chart that plots process results over time against a center line and upper/lower control limits.
items.whyItMatters: High-value PMP diagram for interpreting stability, special-cause variation, and out-of-control conditions.
items.howToReadIt: Look for points outside the control limits or non-random patterns that suggest the process is unstable.
items.commonTrap: Control limits are often confused with specification limits.
items.memoryHook: Control chart = is the process stable?

items.title: Histogram
items.whatItIs: A frequency-distribution chart showing how often values fall within defined ranges.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for visualizing spread, clustering, and data distribution in quality questions.
items.howToReadIt: Read the height of each bin/bar to understand where observations cluster.
items.commonTrap: Unlike a Pareto chart, the bars are not ordered by importance.
items.memoryHook: Histogram = shape of the data.

items.title: Scatter Diagram
items.whatItIs: A plot of two variables used to observe whether a relationship or correlation may exist.
items.whyItMatters: Important when a PMP question asks whether one factor appears related to another.
items.howToReadIt: Look for upward, downward, or no clear pattern among plotted points.
items.commonTrap: Correlation is not proof of causation.
items.memoryHook: Scatter = are these moving together?

items.title: Probability-Impact Matrix
items.whatItIs: A risk heat map classifying risks by probability and impact.
items.whyItMatters: Very useful for qualitative risk analysis and prioritization.
items.howToReadIt: Locate each risk on the matrix to see which ones need the greatest attention.
items.commonTrap: This prioritizes risks qualitatively; it is not the same as quantitative modeling or a tornado diagram.
items.memoryHook: Risk matrix = how likely and how big?

items.title: Tornado Diagram
items.whatItIs: A sensitivity-analysis bar chart showing which variables have the greatest effect on an outcome.
items.whyItMatters: Useful in risk and quantitative analysis questions to identify the biggest uncertainty drivers.
items.howToReadIt: The longest bars matter most. Read from top to bottom to see which variable swings the result the most.
items.commonTrap: Students confuse it with a risk register or probability-impact matrix. A tornado diagram shows impact sensitivity, not a list of risks.
items.memoryHook: Tornado = what shakes the outcome most.

items.title: Decision Tree
items.whatItIs: A branching diagram showing decision options, chance outcomes, and expected values.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for EMV and decision-analysis questions.
items.howToReadIt: Read from left to right through decisions and chance events, then compare expected outcomes.
items.commonTrap: Students often forget to multiply outcome by probability when interpreting branches.
items.memoryHook: Decision tree = options + uncertainty + value.

items.title: Network Diagram / Critical Path
items.whatItIs: A project schedule logic diagram showing activities, dependencies, and the path that determines project duration.
items.whyItMatters: Foundational for critical-path and float questions.
items.howToReadIt: Follow the sequence of dependent activities and identify the longest path.
items.commonTrap: Learners sometimes focus on the visually busiest path rather than the longest duration path.
items.memoryHook: Critical path = longest duration path.

items.title: Burndown Chart
items.whatItIs: A chart showing remaining work declining over time within a sprint or release.
items.whyItMatters: Useful in agile tracking and forecasting questions.
items.howToReadIt: Read whether remaining work is trending down in line with expectations.
items.commonTrap: Burndown shows remaining work, not value delivered.
items.memoryHook: Burndown = work left.

items.title: Burnup Chart
items.whatItIs: A chart showing completed work increasing over time, often against a total-scope line.
items.whyItMatters: Useful when a PMP question asks about progress while total scope may also change.
items.howToReadIt: Read completed work versus total scope, especially if scope expands.
items.commonTrap: Students confuse burnup with burndown. Burnup highlights completed work and scope changes more clearly.
items.memoryHook: Burnup = work done.

items.title: Cumulative Flow Diagram
items.whatItIs: A stacked-flow chart showing work items by state over time.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for seeing bottlenecks, WIP growth, and flow stability in Kanban systems.
items.howToReadIt: Watch the width and spacing between bands; widening bands can signal a bottleneck or growing WIP.
items.commonTrap: Learners may read it like a burndown chart instead of a flow chart by state.
items.memoryHook: Cumulative flow = where work is getting stuck.

items.title: Kanban Board
items.whatItIs: A visual board showing work items across columns such as To Do, In Progress, and Done, often with WIP limits.
items.whyItMatters: Helpful for questions about flow, pull, and limiting multitasking.
items.howToReadIt: Read from left to right and pay special attention to blocked work and WIP-limit violations.
items.commonTrap: A board alone is not enough; WIP limits and flow management are key.
items.memoryHook: Kanban = visualize and limit work in progress.

items.title: Change Control Flow
items.whatItIs: A flow diagram showing change identified → impact analysis → change request → decision → update/communicate → implement → monitor.
items.whyItMatters: Excellent for one of the most frequently tested PMP decision patterns.
items.howToReadIt: Read the sequence carefully. Impact analysis comes before approval and certainly before implementation.
items.commonTrap: The biggest trap is implementing first because the sponsor or customer requested it.
items.memoryHook: Change = analyze before approve; approve before implement.

items.title: Risk-to-Issue Flow
items.whatItIs: A flow showing uncertain future risk moving through analysis and response, and if it occurs, becoming a current issue requiring issue management.
items.whyItMatters: Useful because learners constantly confuse risks and issues.
items.howToReadIt: Read the point at which future uncertainty becomes a present problem.
items.commonTrap: A risk that has occurred should not be managed only as a future risk.
items.memoryHook: Risk may happen; issue has happened.

items.title: Document Map
items.whatItIs: A conceptual map linking Charter, Business Case, Management Plan, Baselines, RTM, WBS Dictionary, Risk Register, Issue Log, Change Log, and Contract.
items.whyItMatters: Useful because many PMP questions test document confusion more than difficult formulas.
items.howToReadIt: Read by function: WHY, AUTHORITY, HOW, APPROVED, TRACE, MAY HAPPEN, HAPPENED, CHANGE STATUS, SELLER.
items.commonTrap: Students select the wrong artifact because names sound similar.
items.memoryHook: Document map = know what each artifact is for.

items.title: Business Need → Business Case → Project → Benefits → Value Chain
items.whatItIs: A chain showing how an organizational problem or opportunity becomes a business case, then a project, then outcomes, benefits, and ultimately value.
items.whyItMatters: Important because PMP often tests the difference between finishing deliverables and creating real business value.
items.howToReadIt: Read left to right. Delivery is not the end; value realization continues beyond project completion.
items.commonTrap: A completed project does not automatically equal realized value.
items.memoryHook: Deliverable is not value; value comes later.

items.title: Governance Escalation Path
items.whatItIs: A diagram showing issue assessment, authority check, decision owner, action, and escalation path.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for questions about who should decide and when escalation is appropriate.
items.howToReadIt: Read the authority checkpoints: solve at the lowest appropriate level, escalate when authority or governance requires it.
items.commonTrap: Escalation is often chosen too early before understanding the issue or checking authority.
items.memoryHook: Governance = know who decides what.

items.title: Organizational Change Adoption Flow
items.whatItIs: A people-centered flow showing understand resistance → engage → communicate → train → reinforce adoption.
items.whyItMatters: Useful when questions concern user adoption, resistance, and benefits realization rather than simple baseline change.
items.howToReadIt: Read the flow as an adoption journey, not as formal change control.
items.commonTrap: Students often confuse organizational change management with integrated change control.
items.memoryHook: Adoption is a people journey, not just a project form.

items.title: Compliance Decision Flow
items.whatItIs: A flow showing identify compliance issue → assess impact → consult required authority/expert → update/implement → document.
items.whyItMatters: Useful when a scenario involves legal, regulatory, safety, or policy constraints.
items.howToReadIt: Read compliance as mandatory and non-optional, then see how response flows through governance and documentation.
items.commonTrap: Learners often trade away compliance for cost or schedule as if it were negotiable.
items.memoryHook: Compliance is mandatory, not a preference.

items.title: Finance Formula Family Map
items.whatItIs: A visual grouping of ROI, BCR, NPV, IRR, Payback, Opportunity Cost, Sunk Cost, CAPEX, OPEX, and TCO.
items.whyItMatters: Useful because finance questions are often hard due to concept confusion rather than calculation difficulty.
items.howToReadIt: Read by purpose: profitability, time-to-recovery, value today, rate of return, cost classification, and decision-quality concepts.
items.commonTrap: Students treat all metrics as interchangeable when they answer different questions.
items.memoryHook: Finance map = choose the right metric for the decision.

items.title: AI Decision-Support Flow
items.whatItIs: A flow showing data check → privacy/security check → generate insight → validate output → human decision.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for modern PMP-style governance and responsible AI scenarios.
items.howToReadIt: Read it as decision support. AI can assist, but humans remain accountable.
items.commonTrap: Treating AI output as authoritative without verification is the core trap.
items.memoryHook: AI helps decide; humans own the decision.

items.title: Sustainability Triple-Bottom-Line Diagram
items.whatItIs: A visual showing environmental, social, and economic considerations balanced together.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for questions that test long-term value and responsible decision making.
items.howToReadIt: Read the overlap and the need to balance lifecycle impact, not merely optimize upfront cost.
items.commonTrap: Learners may choose the cheapest option even when sustainability criteria clearly matter.
items.memoryHook: Sustainability = people + planet + economics.

items.title: Project vs Program vs Portfolio vs Operations Map
items.whatItIs: A comparison visual distinguishing temporary project work, coordinated program benefits, strategic portfolio alignment, and ongoing operations.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for foundational classification questions.
items.howToReadIt: Read each item by its main purpose: outcome, benefits, strategy, or run-the-business continuity.
items.commonTrap: A program is not just a very big project, and a portfolio does not require all work to be directly related.
items.memoryHook: Project = outcome; Program = benefits; Portfolio = strategy; Operations = ongoing work.

items.title: Stakeholder Salience Model
items.whatItIs: A three-circle stakeholder model using power, legitimacy, and urgency to identify stakeholder salience.
items.whyItMatters: Helps prioritize stakeholder attention when influence, rightful involvement, and time sensitivity differ.
items.howToReadIt: Read the overlap of power, legitimacy, and urgency; stakeholders with all three attributes are definitive and normally require the highest attention.
items.commonTrap: Do not confuse salience with the power/interest grid; salience uses three attributes rather than two.
items.memoryHook: Salience = Power + Legitimacy + Urgency.

items.title: Organizational Breakdown Structure (OBS)
items.whatItIs: A hierarchical view of organizational units, departments, or teams responsible for project work.
items.whyItMatters: Helps learners distinguish organization-based responsibility structures from deliverable-based decomposition.
items.howToReadIt: Read from the organization or enterprise down through divisions, departments, and teams.
items.commonTrap: OBS is organization-based; WBS is deliverable/work based.
items.memoryHook: OBS = who in the organization; WBS = what work.

items.title: Organizational Structure Comparison
items.whatItIs: A comparison of functional, weak/balanced/strong matrix, and projectized structures.
items.whyItMatters: Shows how project manager authority, resource control, and team alignment change across structures.
items.howToReadIt: Move from functional toward projectized to see project-manager authority generally increase and functional control generally decrease.
items.commonTrap: Matrix is not one structure; weak, balanced, and strong matrix give different authority levels.
items.memoryHook: Functional → Matrix → Projectized = generally more PM authority.

items.title: Communication Model
items.whatItIs: A sender-to-receiver communication model showing encoding, message/channel, decoding, noise, and feedback.
items.whyItMatters: Useful for questions involving misunderstanding, communication barriers, feedback, and channel selection.
items.howToReadIt: Follow sender → encode → message/channel → decode → receiver, then use feedback to confirm understanding while watching for noise.
items.commonTrap: A message being sent does not mean it was understood.
items.memoryHook: Send → Encode → Channel → Decode → Confirm.

items.title: Motivation Theory Comparison
items.whatItIs: A comparison of McGregor Theory X/Y, Herzberg, McClelland, and Vroom motivation concepts.
items.whyItMatters: Helps distinguish different explanations of what drives behavior and how leaders can respond.
items.howToReadIt: Compare each theory by its core assumption, primary motivators, and appropriate leadership application.
items.commonTrap: Do not assume one motivator works for every person or every situation.
items.memoryHook: Motivation = diagnose the person and context first.

items.title: Situational Leadership
items.whatItIs: A situational leadership model comparing directing, coaching, supporting, and delegating based on direction and support needs.
items.whyItMatters: Reinforces that leadership style should change as team capability, confidence, and context change.
items.howToReadIt: Match the team member’s development/readiness needs to the amount of directive and supportive behavior required.
items.commonTrap: There is no universally best leadership style; the appropriate style depends on readiness and context.
items.memoryHook: Adapt the leader to the learner.

items.title: Decision-Making Style Spectrum
items.whatItIs: A continuum from leader-decides through consultation and collaboration to delegated team decisions.
items.whyItMatters: Helps select an appropriate decision approach based on urgency, expertise, commitment, reversibility, and authority.
items.howToReadIt: Move from centralized to participative decision making as team involvement increases and direct leader control decreases.
items.commonTrap: Consensus is not automatically best when urgency or authority requires a faster decision.
items.memoryHook: Decision style follows context, authority, urgency, and commitment.

items.title: Gantt Chart
items.whatItIs: A time-phased bar chart showing tasks, start/finish dates, durations, and often dependencies.
items.whyItMatters: Makes schedule timing, overlap, sequence, and progress visible.
items.howToReadIt: Read activities vertically and time horizontally; each bar shows when an activity occurs and for how long.
items.commonTrap: A Gantt chart shows timing; it does not by itself prove which path is critical unless dependency logic is analyzed.
items.memoryHook: Gantt = work across time.

items.title: Crashing vs. Fast-Tracking
items.whatItIs: A visual comparison of two schedule-compression techniques: adding resources/cost versus overlapping work.
items.whyItMatters: Many schedule questions require selecting the right compression technique and recognizing its trade-offs.
items.howToReadIt: Crashing adds resources to shorten critical-path work; fast-tracking overlaps activities that were planned sequentially.
items.commonTrap: Crashing generally increases cost; fast-tracking generally increases rework/coordination risk.
items.memoryHook: Crash = cost; Fast-track = overlap/risk.

items.title: EVM S-Curve
items.whatItIs: A cumulative performance chart plotting Planned Value (PV), Earned Value (EV), and Actual Cost (AC) over time.
items.whyItMatters: Allows visual interpretation of cost and schedule performance and connects directly to CPI, SPI, forecasts, and variance formulas.
items.howToReadIt: At the status date compare EV with AC for cost performance and EV with PV for schedule performance.
items.commonTrap: SPI is EV/PV and CPI is EV/AC; do not reverse the denominators.
items.memoryHook: EV vs AC = cost; EV vs PV = schedule.

items.title: Cost Baseline vs. Actual Cost Curve
items.whatItIs: A cumulative-cost comparison between the approved cost baseline and actual spending over time.
items.whyItMatters: Shows whether spending is above or below the planned cost path and supports investigation and forecasting.
items.howToReadIt: Compare the actual-cost curve to the baseline at the same date; then combine with EV when judging full performance.
items.commonTrap: Actual cost below baseline does not automatically mean good performance if less work was completed; use EV for full analysis.
items.memoryHook: Cost curve shows spend; EV shows value earned.

items.title: Work Breakdown Structure (WBS)
items.whatItIs: A hierarchical decomposition of total project scope into deliverables and progressively smaller components/work packages.
items.whyItMatters: Supports scope completeness, estimating, planning, ownership, and control.
items.howToReadIt: Read top-down from project/deliverable to lower-level components; the hierarchy represents scope, not schedule order.
items.commonTrap: WBS hierarchy is not the same as activity sequence.
items.memoryHook: WBS = break the work, not the timeline.

items.title: Risk Register Structure
items.whatItIs: A structured table for identified risks, causes, impacts, probability, responses, owners, triggers, and status.
items.whyItMatters: Shows how risks are documented, owned, monitored, and updated through the project.
items.howToReadIt: Read each row as one risk with its assessment and planned response; monitor ownership, triggers, and status.
items.commonTrap: An issue that has already occurred belongs in issue management even if it originated as a risk.
items.memoryHook: Risk register = identify, assess, respond, own, monitor.

items.title: Flowchart / Process Map
items.whatItIs: A step-by-step visual representation of activities, decisions, branches, and process flow.
items.whyItMatters: Helps learners trace process logic, identify decision points, and understand sequence and rework loops.
items.howToReadIt: Start at the beginning and follow arrows through activities and decision diamonds to the appropriate endpoint.
items.commonTrap: A flowchart shows sequence; a context diagram shows system boundaries and external interfaces.
items.memoryHook: Flowchart = what happens next?

items.title: Earned Schedule (ES) & SPI(t)
items.whatItIs: A time-based schedule performance technique that converts earned progress into the point in planned time when that amount of value was expected.
items.whyItMatters: Adds a time-based schedule view using Earned Schedule and SPI(t), especially useful for interpreting schedule performance in time units.
items.howToReadIt: Find current EV, project it to the PV curve to locate Earned Schedule (ES), then compare ES with actual time/status date (AT). SPI(t)=ES/AT.
items.commonTrap: Traditional SPI is EV/PV; SPI(t) is ES/AT.
items.memoryHook: Earned Schedule asks: how far along in planned time have we actually earned?

items.title: Cost of Quality (COQ)
items.whatItIs: A framework dividing quality costs into conformance costs (prevention/appraisal) and nonconformance costs (internal/external failure).
items.whyItMatters: Shows why investing in prevention and appraisal can reduce expensive failure costs.
items.howToReadIt: Separate doing-it-right costs from failure costs, then distinguish failures found internally from those found by customers.
items.commonTrap: Quality cost includes the cost of achieving quality as well as the cost of poor quality.
items.memoryHook: Prevent + Appraise before Internal + External Failure.

items.title: Velocity Chart
items.whatItIs: A sprint-by-sprint chart of completed work, commonly story points, used for team planning and forecasting.
items.whyItMatters: Helps a stable team forecast likely future capacity based on its own recent empirical performance.
items.howToReadIt: Compare completed points across sprints and use recent trends/ranges rather than assuming a perfectly constant number.
items.commonTrap: Do not compare velocity across teams or use it as an individual productivity score.
items.memoryHook: Velocity forecasts this team, not every team.

items.title: Backlog Hierarchy & Prioritization Flow
items.whatItIs: A visual hierarchy from product vision/goal through epics, features/capabilities, backlog items/user stories, and tasks, plus the factors used to order work.
items.whyItMatters: Connects decomposition with continuous value-based reprioritization and progressive refinement.
items.howToReadIt: Move from strategic intent toward smaller implementable items; use value, risk, dependencies, compliance, learning, and effort to order upcoming work.
items.commonTrap: The backlog is ordered and continuously refined; it is not a frozen scope list.
items.memoryHook: Vision → Epic → Feature → Story → Task; then reorder with learning.

items.title: Contract Type Risk Spectrum
items.whatItIs: A comparison of common contract types and how cost risk is allocated between buyer and seller.
items.whyItMatters: Supports procurement questions about scope certainty, incentives, flexibility, and who bears financial risk.
items.howToReadIt: Compare fixed-price and cost-reimbursable families by cost-risk allocation; treat T&M as a flexible hybrid arrangement rather than a simple endpoint.
items.commonTrap: T&M is not automatically the highest-risk endpoint of a single spectrum; it combines fixed rates with variable quantity/time exposure.
items.memoryHook: Clear scope favors fixed price; uncertainty often shifts more cost risk to the buyer.

items.title: Predictive vs. Agile vs. Hybrid
items.whatItIs: A side-by-side comparison of predictive, adaptive/agile, and hybrid delivery across planning, requirements, change, cadence, stakeholder involvement, and governance.
items.whyItMatters: Reinforces tailoring: different work benefits from different delivery approaches.
items.howToReadIt: Compare uncertainty, planning horizon, delivery cadence, change handling, and stakeholder feedback to choose the best-fit approach.
items.commonTrap: No approach is universally best; choose based on uncertainty, complexity, risk, governance, and organizational context.
items.memoryHook: Stable → predictive; uncertain → adaptive; mixed → hybrid.
